title: PANCE
issuer: National Commission on Certification of Physician Assistants
content_provenance: Original practice items authored from the public PANCE content blueprint. Not a capture of past test questions.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man presents with 2 hours of crushing substernal chest pain, diaphoresis, and nausea. The ECG shows 3 mm ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF with reciprocal ST depression in leads I and aVL. Which coronary artery is most likely occluded?
options: Left circumflex artery
Right coronary artery
Left anterior descending artery
Left main coronary artery
items.explanation: Inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction with reciprocal lateral changes is the classic pattern of right coronary artery occlusion, while the other vessels produce anterior or lateral injury patterns.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Cardiovascular and Respiratory

items.stem: A 74-year-old woman reports progressive orthopnea requiring three pillows, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and bilateral leg swelling. Examination shows elevated jugular venous pressure, an S3 gallop, and bibasilar crackles. Echocardiography shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 24 percent with global hypokinesis. Which diagnosis best fits these findings?
options: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
Isolated chronic kidney disease with volume overload
Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
Constrictive pericarditis
items.explanation: Congestive symptoms plus an ejection fraction well below 40 percent with global hypokinesis define heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, whereas preserved-fraction failure would show a fraction above 50 percent.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Cardiovascular and Respiratory

items.stem: A 58-year-old man is noted to have a rapid, irregularly irregular pulse at 140 beats per minute during a routine visit. The ECG shows no discernible P waves, an irregular ventricular response, and no sawtooth baseline. Which rhythm is present?
options: Multifocal atrial tachycardia
Sinus tachycardia with frequent premature beats
Typical atrial flutter with variable block
Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
items.explanation: An irregularly irregular narrow-complex tachycardia without identifiable P waves or flutter waves is atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular conduction.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Cardiovascular and Respiratory

items.stem: A 66-year-old man with hypertension and diabetes has had rest angina for 18 hours. The ECG shows 2 mm horizontal ST depression in six leads, and serial high-sensitivity troponin values are rising. He is hemodynamically stable with no bleeding. Which management strategy is most appropriate?
options: Outpatient exercise stress testing within one week
Coronary angiography with revascularization within 24 hours
Immediate systemic fibrinolytic therapy
Elective surgical revascularization scheduled in three months
items.explanation: Ongoing ischemia with dynamic ST depression and a rising troponin marks a high-risk non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome, which warrants an early invasive strategy rather than fibrinolysis or deferred testing.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Cardiovascular and Respiratory

items.stem: A 45-year-old man with exertional syncope has a harsh late-peaking crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to both carotids, a delayed and diminished carotid upstroke, and a soft S2. Which valvular lesion is most likely?
options: Calcific aortic stenosis
Chronic severe mitral regurgitation
Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy
Aortic regurgitation
items.explanation: Exertional syncope with a late-peaking murmur radiating to the carotids and a soft S2 indicates severe aortic stenosis, while regurgitation would instead widen the pulse pressure.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Cardiovascular and Respiratory

items.stem: An 80-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation maintained on digoxin presents with nausea, confusion, and yellow-tinged visual halos. Her serum potassium is 3.2 mmol per liter and her digoxin concentration is 4.8 ng per mL. Which intervention is most appropriate?
options: Oral potassium replacement while continuing the usual digoxin dose
Intravenous calcium gluconate to stabilize the myocardium
Immediate electrical cardioversion of the atrial fibrillation
Discontinuation of digoxin with administration of digoxin-immune Fab
items.explanation: Visual symptoms at a supratherapeutic level require stopping the drug and binding digoxin with immune Fab, since hypokalemia worsens toxicity and cardioversion here can provoke ventricular arrhythmias.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Cardiovascular and Respiratory

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman reports cough and chest tightness requiring albuterol on three days per week and awakenings on three nights per month, with no activity limitation. Spirometry shows an FEV1 of 92 percent of predicted with a 13 percent and 210 mL improvement after bronchodilator. Which asthma category applies?
options: Mild intermittent asthma
Moderate persistent asthma
Mild persistent asthma
Severe persistent asthma
items.explanation: Symptoms on more than two days per week but not daily, with nighttime awakenings three to four times per month and preserved FEV1, meet criteria for mild persistent asthma.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Cardiovascular and Respiratory

items.stem: A 68-year-old with COPD is admitted with increased dyspnea and purulent sputum. Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shows pH 7.31, PaCO2 58 mm Hg, and bicarbonate 28 mmol per liter, and he is drowsy but arousable with no contraindication to mask ventilation. Which initial therapy is most appropriate?
options: Noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation with controlled oxygen, nebulized bronchodilators, and systemic corticosteroids
Ambulatory oxygen titration without additional acute therapy
Immediate endotracheal intubation and invasive mechanical ventilation
High-flow 100 percent oxygen by non-rebreather with no ventilatory support
items.explanation: Acute hypercapnic respiratory failure with a pH below 7.35 in an arousable patient without contraindications is the classic indication for noninvasive ventilation, with intubation reserved for failure.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Cardiovascular and Respiratory

items.stem: A 34-year-old previously healthy man develops a necrotizing cavitary pneumonia with septic physiology five days after laboratory-confirmed influenza infection. Sputum culture grows gram-positive cocci in clusters that are methicillin-resistant. Which organism is responsible?
options: Klebsiella pneumoniae
Haemophilus influenzae
Streptococcus pneumoniae
Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus
items.explanation: Post-influenza necrotizing pneumonia yielding methicillin-resistant gram-positive cocci in clusters is Staphylococcus aureus, the organism most associated with cavitary lung destruction after influenza.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Cardiovascular and Respiratory

items.stem: On postoperative day 4 after hip replacement, a 55-year-old woman develops pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia at 120 beats per minute, and hypotension at 84/58 mm Hg. CT pulmonary angiography shows a saddle embolus with right ventricular dilation. Which intervention is most appropriate?
options: Unfractionated heparin bolus without reperfusion therapy
Placement of an inferior vena cava filter alone
Supportive care with repeat imaging in 24 hours
Systemic thrombolytic therapy
items.explanation: High-risk pulmonary embolism with shock and right heart strain carries high mortality and demands immediate systemic reperfusion, with anticoagulation begun alongside it but insufficient by itself.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Cardiovascular and Respiratory

items.stem: A 48-year-old woman has hypertension requiring three agents, serum potassium of 3.0 mmol per liter, metabolic alkalosis, and intermittent muscle weakness. She denies licorice, supplement, or diuretic use. Which test best establishes the diagnosis?
options: Twenty-four hour urine catecholamines and metanephrines
Renal artery duplex ultrasonography
Plasma aldosterone concentration measured with concurrent plasma renin activity
Short cosyntropin stimulation test
items.explanation: Resistant hypertension with spontaneous hypokalemia and alkalosis points to primary aldosteronism, for which a high aldosterone with suppressed renin is the appropriate screening test.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Cardiovascular and Respiratory

items.stem: A 66-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy has a left ventricular ejection fraction of 28 percent and New York Heart Association class III symptoms despite optimized therapy with a beta blocker, an ACE inhibitor, and a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist. His ECG shows sinus rhythm with left bundle branch block and QRS duration of 166 ms. Which device is indicated?
options: Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator without resynchronization
Cardiac resynchronization therapy defibrillator
Insertable cardiac monitor only
Permanent dual-chamber pacemaker without defibrillator capability
items.explanation: Marked LV systolic dysfunction with class III symptoms and a left bundle branch block of at least 150 ms on guideline-directed therapy meets criteria for resynchronization with defibrillator backup.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Cardiovascular and Respiratory

items.stem: A 58-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension reports sudden severe tearing pain radiating to the interscapular region. Blood pressure is 186/102 in the right arm and 142/84 in the left, and a new diastolic murmur is heard. Which study should be obtained first to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Computed tomography angiography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis
Exercise treadmill stress testing
Transthoracic echocardiography without any cross-sectional imaging
D-dimer measurement to exclude acute aortic syndrome
items.explanation: Suspected acute aortic syndrome requires immediate cross-sectional imaging of the entire aorta, and CT angiography is the fastest confirmatory study; stress testing and d-dimer are inappropriate in an unstable patient.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Cardiovascular and Respiratory

items.stem: A 22-year-old tall smoker presents with sudden right-sided pleuritic pain and mild dyspnea after a coughing spell. He is comfortable, saturation is 96 percent on room air, and the radiograph shows a 1.5 cm apical pneumothorax without mediastinal shift. Which management is most appropriate?
options: Supplemental oxygen with observation and repeat radiography
Empirical antibiotics with admission
Tube thoracostomy in the emergency department
Emergent video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery
items.explanation: A small primary spontaneous pneumothorax in a stable patient can be observed with supplemental oxygen and serial imaging, because oxygen accelerates reabsorption and most small collections resolve.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Cardiovascular and Respiratory

items.stem: A 68-year-old former smoker has 9 months of progressive exertional dyspnea and dry cough. Examination reveals bibasilar velcro crackles and digital clubbing. Pulmonary function tests show a restrictive pattern with reduced DLCO, and high-resolution CT shows subpleural honeycombing with traction bronchiectasis. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis
Pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis
Sarcoidosis
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis with a usual interstitial pneumonia pattern
items.explanation: An older smoker with clubbing, restrictive physiology with reduced diffusing capacity, and subpleural honeycombing has usual interstitial pneumonia consistent with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Cardiovascular and Respiratory

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman with osteoarthritis presents with melena and fatigue. Endoscopy shows a 10 mm gastric ulcer with a clean base and no adherent clot after bleeding was treated. Hemoglobin is 9.0 g per dL and she is hemodynamically stable. Which next step is most appropriate?
options: Repeat endoscopy every 12 hours for 48 hours
Immediate percutaneous angiographic embolization
High-dose proton pump inhibitor therapy, withdrawal of the NSAID, and oral iron
Emergent partial gastrectomy
items.explanation: A clean-based ulcer that has stopped bleeding is low risk, so the priorities are acid suppression, removing the offending NSAID, and replacing iron, while surgery and repeat endoscopy await rebleeding.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Gastrointestinal and Genitourinary

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman has 14 hours of periumbilical pain migrating to the right lower quadrant with anorexia and low-grade fever. CT shows a 10 mm non-perforated appendix with periappendiceal fat stranding, and she tolerates oral liquids with stable vital signs. Which management is preferred?
options: Observation with serial abdominal examinations only
Laparoscopic appendectomy
Percutaneous drainage of the appendiceal base
Colonoscopy in six weeks to exclude malignancy
items.explanation: CT-confirmed uncomplicated acute appendicitis in a stable patient is treated with appendectomy, which lowers the risk of perforation compared with observation alone.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Gastrointestinal and Genitourinary

items.stem: A 50-year-old immunocompetent man has left lower quadrant pain, temperature of 37.9 C, and CT findings of uncomplicated sigmoid diverticulitis without abscess or free air. He tolerates oral intake with stable vital signs. Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Emergency sigmoid resection
Oral antibiotics with a clear liquid diet and close outpatient follow-up
CT-guided percutaneous drainage of the affected segment
Immediate colonoscopy during the acute episode
items.explanation: Uncomplicated diverticulitis without abscess or perforation in a reliable outpatient is managed with oral antibiotics and dietary restriction, while colonoscopy is deferred until acute inflammation resolves.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Gastrointestinal and Genitourinary

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman with known choledocholithiasis presents with right upper quadrant pain, fever to 39 C, and jaundice, then becomes hypotensive with altered mental status. Leukocytosis and a markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase are noted. Which intervention is most urgent?
options: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography with urgent biliary decompression
Elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy later in the week
Percutaneous transhepatic cholangiogram as the initial diagnostic test
Broad-spectrum antibiotics alone with watchful waiting
items.explanation: Ascending cholangitis progressing to shock is biliary sepsis, and drainage of the common bile duct is the source control that must not be delayed, with resuscitation and antibiotics running in parallel.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Gastrointestinal and Genitourinary

items.stem: A 44-year-old man with chronic alcohol use presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, and vomiting. Lipase is 1,250 units per liter, hematocrit is 47 percent, blood urea nitrogen is rising, and he is tachycardic with borderline hypotension. Which initial management is best?
options: Aggressive early resuscitation with isotonic crystalloid
Early total parenteral nutrition by central catheter
Immediate endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography
Prophylactic broad-spectrum antibiotics regardless of any sign of infection
items.explanation: Early aggressive isotonic crystalloid is the cornerstone of acute pancreatitis resuscitation because it reduces necrosis, while endoscopy is reserved for biliary obstruction and prophylactic antibiotics show no benefit.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Gastrointestinal and Genitourinary

items.stem: A 58-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis gains 5 kg over 2 weeks with tense ascites and bilateral leg edema. Serum sodium is 135 mmol per liter and creatinine is unchanged from baseline. Which diuretic regimen is the standard initial therapy?
options: Acetazolamide as the sole agent
Metolazone alone before any aldosterone blockade
Intravenous furosemide as monotherapy
Oral spironolactone combined with furosemide
items.explanation: Ascites in cirrhosis is driven by secondary hyperaldosteronism, so aldosterone blockade with spironolactone plus a loop diuretic is first line and the pairing limits potassium loss.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Gastrointestinal and Genitourinary

items.stem: A 61-year-old man with cirrhosis and prior bleeding esophageal varices has completed endoscopic band ligation to variceal eradication. His MELD score is 14 and he has no contraindication to beta blockade. Which strategy best prevents rebleeding?
options: Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt as routine first-line therapy for every patient
Anticoagulation with a direct oral anticoagulant to prevent portal vein thrombosis
Nonselective beta blockade with continued periodic band ligation
Serial band ligation every two weeks indefinitely with no medication
items.explanation: Secondary prophylaxis after variceal bleeding combines a nonselective beta blocker with repeat ligation until varices are gone, while the shunt is reserved for failures and anticoagulation does not lower portal pressure.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Gastrointestinal and Genitourinary

items.stem: A 58-year-old man with hepatitis C-related cirrhosis, Child-Pugh class A, has never undergone hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance and remains a candidate for curative treatment if a tumor is found early. Which surveillance protocol is recommended?
options: Magnetic resonance imaging of the liver every 2 years
Liver ultrasonography with alpha-fetoprotein every 6 months
Computed tomography of the abdomen every 12 months
Serum alpha-fetoprotein alone every 3 months
items.explanation: Guidelines call for ultrasound with alpha-fetoprotein every 6 months in cirrhosis because that interval balances early detection against cost, with CT and MRI reserved for following up positive screens.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Gastrointestinal and Genitourinary

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman with iron-deficiency anemia unresponsive to oral iron, chronic diarrhea, and a 6 kg weight loss undergoes duodenal biopsy showing villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes. Which serologic test best supports the diagnosis while she continues to eat gluten?
options: Anti-endomysial antibody of the IgG subclass
Fecal calprotectin measurement
Serum anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibodies
Tissue transglutaminase IgA measured with a concurrent total serum IgA level
items.explanation: Tissue transglutaminase IgA is the preferred screening test for celiac disease, but a total IgA level must accompany it because IgA deficiency would otherwise yield a falsely negative result.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Gastrointestinal and Genitourinary

items.stem: A 30-year-old man has 3 months of bloody diarrhea, tenesmus, and abdominal cramping with a 5 kg weight loss and elevated C-reactive protein. Colonoscopy shows continuous erythema and friability extending from the rectum into the descending colon with a normal terminal ileum. Which feature best supports the diagnosis?
options: Non-caseating granulomas on biopsy
Skip lesions with cobblestoning and transmural inflammation
Continuous mucosal inflammation beginning at the rectum with crypt abscesses
Small bowel strictures on capsule endoscopy with a normal colon
items.explanation: Continuous inflammation starting at the rectum with crypt abscesses is ulcerative colitis, whereas skip lesions, cobblestoning, and transmural granulomas characterize Crohn disease.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Gastrointestinal and Genitourinary

items.stem: A 45-year-old average-risk man undergoes screening colonoscopy, which removes three tubular adenomas, the largest 8 mm, all with low-grade dysplasia and no villous features. He has no family history of colorectal cancer. When should surveillance colonoscopy be repeated?
options: Within 6 months to confirm complete resection
In 3 to 5 years
In 7 to 10 years
In 10 years with no further testing
items.explanation: Three to four adenomas all smaller than 10 mm without high-grade dysplasia place him in the intermediate surveillance group, which calls for repeat examination in 3 to 5 years.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Gastrointestinal and Genitourinary

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman is evaluated for recurrent urinary tract infections and a staghorn calculus. Urine culture grows a gram-negative rod that splits urea and produces alkaline urine, and stone analysis confirms struvite. Which organism is most likely?
options: Proteus mirabilis
Staphylococcus saprophyticus
Escherichia coli
Enterococcus faecalis
items.explanation: Urea-splitting organisms raise urine pH and promote struvite stones, and Proteus mirabilis is the classic cause of infection-induced staghorn calculi while the other organisms do not split urea.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Gastrointestinal and Genitourinary

items.stem: A 68-year-old man reports weak stream, hesitancy, nocturia four times nightly, and incomplete emptying for 18 months. The prostate is smooth and moderately enlarged, PSA is 1.2 ng per mL, post-void residual is 90 mL, and he has no recurrent infection or renal insufficiency. Which medication offers the most rapid symptom relief?
options: Oxybutynin, an antimuscarinic
Propranolol, a nonselective beta blocker
Tamsulosin, an alpha-1 adrenergic blocker
Finasteride, a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor
items.explanation: Alpha-1 blockade relaxes prostatic smooth muscle and relieves symptoms within days, whereas 5-alpha reductase inhibitors take months to shrink the gland and anticholinergics can worsen emptying.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Gastrointestinal and Genitourinary

items.stem: A 55-year-old man with cirrhosis presents with new confusion and asterixis two days after a variceal bleed, and serum ammonia is elevated. In addition to controlling the bleeding source, which regimen is most appropriate for the encephalopathy?
options: Sodium polystyrene sulfonate directed at the potassium level
Lactulose titrated to produce loose stools with rifaximin added
Neomycin monotherapy for seven days
Intravenous mannitol to reduce cerebral edema
items.explanation: Overt hepatic encephalopathy is treated with lactulose to clear ammonia through the gut and rifaximin to reduce recurrence, while neomycin is no longer preferred as sole therapy.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Gastrointestinal and Genitourinary

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman has 6 months of intermittent heartburn and regurgitation with no weight loss, dysphagia, anemia, or vomiting, and she improves only partially with antacids. Which initial approach is most appropriate?
options: Immediate computed tomography of the chest and abdomen
Once-daily proton pump inhibitor before breakfast for 4 to 8 weeks with lifestyle measures
Urgent upper endoscopy before any therapy is started
Twenty-four hour ambulatory esophageal pH monitoring before treatment
items.explanation: Typical reflux symptoms without alarm features warrant an empirical proton pump inhibitor trial with lifestyle changes, while endoscopy and pH testing are reserved for refractory or alarm presentations.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Gastrointestinal and Genitourinary

items.stem: A 24-year-old man falls on an outstretched hand and has radial-sided wrist pain with tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox. Initial radiographs show no fracture and there is no neurovascular deficit. Which management is most appropriate?
options: Thumb-spica immobilization with repeat radiography in 10 to 14 days
Immediate magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and cervical spine
Early range-of-motion exercises with return to contact sport in one week
Open reduction and internal fixation without further imaging
items.explanation: Scaphoid fractures are often invisible at first, so snuffbox tenderness requires immobilization and repeat imaging, with advanced imaging if symptoms persist, because missed injuries end in nonunion.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Musculoskeletal and Neurologic

items.stem: An 82-year-old woman who walks with a cane falls and develops a shortened, externally rotated left leg with pain on gentle log-rolling. Radiographs show a displaced femoral neck fracture. Which treatment is preferred?
options: Prolonged skin traction followed by supervised rehabilitation
Closed reduction with percutaneous screw fixation
Extended bed rest with analgesia until callus forms
Total hip arthroplasty
items.explanation: A displaced femoral neck fracture in an ambulatory older adult is treated with arthroplasty because it permits immediate weight bearing and avoids the high rates of nonunion and avascular necrosis after fixation.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Musculoskeletal and Neurologic

items.stem: A 34-year-old man has 6 weeks of low back pain with right leg pain in an L5 distribution, normal strength and reflexes, and no bowel or bladder dysfunction. Conservative care has failed. Which finding would mandate urgent imaging and surgical consultation?
options: Pain that worsens with coughing or sneezing
Mild paraspinal muscle spasm on examination
New saddle anesthesia with urinary retention
A positive straight-leg raise test on the right
items.explanation: Saddle anesthesia with urinary retention signals cauda equina syndrome, a surgical emergency, while the other findings are typical of uncomplicated radiculopathy and need no urgent intervention.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Musculoskeletal and Neurologic

items.stem: A 26-year-old man sustains a forcibly abducted and externally rotated shoulder during a rugby match. The arm is held abducted and externally rotated, the deltoid contour is lost, and neurovascular examination is intact. What is the next step?
options: Computed tomography before any attempt at reduction
Arthroscopic labrum repair during the same admission
Closed reduction with post-reduction radiographs and sling immobilization
Immediate open reduction through a deltopectoral approach
items.explanation: An acute anterior shoulder dislocation with intact neurovasculature is reduced closed and confirmed with radiographs, with arthroscopic repair reserved for recurrent instability.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Musculoskeletal and Neurologic

items.stem: A 38-year-old man with a closed tibial shaft fracture reports pain out of proportion to the injury, pain with passive stretching of the toes, and paresthesias. The limb is tense and capillary refill is 3 seconds. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Wait for an absent Doppler signal before acting
Emergent fasciotomy
Elevate the limb and reassess sensation in one hour
Apply a compressive wrap to reduce swelling
items.explanation: Pain out of proportion with pain on passive stretch and delayed refill is acute compartment syndrome, and the definitive treatment is fasciotomy within hours to prevent muscle and nerve death.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Musculoskeletal and Neurologic

items.stem: A 71-year-old woman with diabetes and fever has an acutely swollen, exquisitely tender, warm right knee with limited passive motion and a leukocyte count of 15,000 per microliter. Joint aspiration yields 80,000 leukocytes per microliter with intracellular organisms on Gram stain. Which management is essential?
options: Arthroscopic irrigation and debridement with intravenous antibiotics
Cast immobilization of the knee for two weeks
Intra-articular corticosteroid injection
Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs with outpatient follow-up
items.explanation: Septic arthritis with a frankly purulent aspirate and organisms on Gram stain needs urgent joint drainage plus antibiotics, because cartilage destruction begins within hours and drugs alone are inadequate.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Musculoskeletal and Neurologic

items.stem: A 67-year-old man develops sudden right-sided weakness and expressive aphasia 90 minutes ago. Non-contrast CT shows no hemorrhage, blood pressure is 182/104, glucose is 108 mg per dL, and there are no contraindications. Which therapy is indicated?
options: Emergent mechanical thrombectomy regardless of vessel findings
Intravenous heparin infusion to prevent propagation
Aspirin with clopidogrel loading in the emergency department
Intravenous alteplase within the treatment window
items.explanation: Disabling ischemic stroke inside the window with a clear CT and no contraindications is treated with intravenous thrombolysis, while antiplatelets wait until hemorrhage is excluded and thrombectomy depends on large vessel imaging.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Musculoskeletal and Neurologic

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis has progressive dyspnea, a weak cough, and inability to count past 15 during serial testing after an upper respiratory infection, with a falling vital capacity. Which intervention is the priority?
options: Home up-titration of oral pyridostigmine without observation
Empirical antibiotics alone with discharge home
Chronic oral prednisone started at a high dose without monitoring
Hospital admission with airway monitoring, noninvasive ventilation, and plasma exchange or intravenous immunoglobulin
items.explanation: Respiratory compromise in myasthenia gravis is a crisis requiring monitored airway support and rapid immunomodulation, because respiratory failure is the leading cause of death in this condition.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Musculoskeletal and Neurologic

items.stem: A 68-year-old man has a 1-year history of asymmetric resting tremor, lead-pipe rigidity, bradykinesia, and a shuffling gait with reduced arm swing. He reports constipation and hyposmia, and his symptoms improve markedly with levodopa. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Essential tremor with secondary parkinsonism
Multiple system atrophy with early autonomic failure
Idiopathic Parkinson disease
Vascular parkinsonism from small vessel disease
items.explanation: Asymmetric resting tremor with rigidity, bradykinesia, prodromal constipation and hyposmia, and clear levodopa responsiveness defines idiopathic Parkinson disease rather than an atypical or drug-induced syndrome.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Musculoskeletal and Neurologic

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman awakens with complete right facial weakness that spares the forehead, altered taste on the anterior tongue, and retroauricular pain, with normal limb strength and sensation. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Myasthenia gravis with isolated ocular involvement
Ramsay Hunt syndrome without any skin lesions
Bell palsy affecting cranial nerve VII
Acute ischemic stroke in the middle cerebral artery territory
items.explanation: Lower motor neuron facial weakness sparing the forehead with ear pain and taste disturbance is Bell palsy, while central stroke spares the forehead because of bilateral cortical innervation.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Musculoskeletal and Neurologic

items.stem: A 19-year-old college student presents with fever to 39.4 C, severe headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, and a petechial rash, with positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs. CSF Gram stain shows gram-negative diplococci. Which empiric therapy should start immediately?
options: Vancomycin alone without gram-negative coverage
Intravenous ceftriaxone with dexamethasone
Oral amoxicillin for presumed viral pharyngitis
Ceftriaxone delayed until culture results return
items.explanation: Suspected bacterial meningitis needs immediate empiric ceftriaxone with adjunctive dexamethasone given with or just before the first dose, because waiting for cultures costs neurologic outcome.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Musculoskeletal and Neurologic

items.stem: A 70-year-old with chronic low back pain reports bilateral leg heaviness after walking one block that improves when he leans forward on a shopping cart, with a negative straight-leg raise and no radicular pattern. Which diagnosis best fits?
options: Lumbar spinal stenosis with neurogenic claudication
Eosinophilic fasciitis with proximal weakness
Lumbar disc herniation with an L4 radiculopathy
Peripheral arterial disease with intermittent claudication
items.explanation: Relief with forward flexion and pain that follows walking rather than posture-independent limits is neurogenic claudication from spinal stenosis, whereas vascular claudication caps distance regardless of position.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Musculoskeletal and Neurologic

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman with a new vertebral compression fracture has a dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry T-score of minus 2.8 at the spine, adequate dietary calcium with vitamin D supplementation, and normal renal function. Which pharmacologic therapy is most appropriate?
options: A parathyroid hormone analog as first-line before any antiresorptive
Two doses of denosumab with no follow-on treatment plan
Conjugated estrogen as the only agent
A bisphosphonate such as alendronate or zoledronic acid
items.explanation: Osteoporosis with a fragility fracture and a T-score at or below minus 2.5 is treated first with a bisphosphonate alongside calcium and vitamin D, while anabolic therapy is reserved for the highest fracture risk.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Musculoskeletal and Neurologic

items.stem: A 25-year-old soccer player pivots and feels a pop, and the knee swells with a hemarthrosis within 2 hours. The Lachman test is positive with a soft endpoint, there is no joint-line tenderness, and the collateral ligaments are stable. Which structure is injured?
options: Medial collateral ligament
Anterior cruciate ligament
Medial meniscus
Posterior cruciate ligament
items.explanation: A hemarthrosis within 2 hours after a pivot with a positive Lachman test indicates an anterior cruciate ligament tear, while meniscal and collateral injuries produce different examination findings.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Musculoskeletal and Neurologic

items.stem: A 9-year-old obese boy has a 3-week history of aching right knee and hip pain with an antalgic gait. Examination shows limited hip abduction and internal rotation with the hip flexed, and the radiograph shows a widened irregular physis with the femoral head displaced posteroinferiorly. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis
Transient synovitis of the hip
Legg-Calve-Perthes disease
Septic arthritis of the hip
items.explanation: An obese adolescent with limp, reduced internal rotation, and posterior inferior displacement of the femoral head through a widened physis has a slipped capital femoral epiphysis, which needs in situ pinning.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Musculoskeletal and Neurologic

items.stem: A 22-year-old with type 1 diabetes reports polyuria and abdominal pain, has Kussmaul respirations and an acetone odor, and labs show glucose 486 mg per dL, anion gap 24, potassium 5.2, bicarbonate 9, and pH 7.15. After initial isotonic fluid resuscitation, which therapy is essential?
options: Metformin at the maximum oral dose
Subcutaneous glargine alone without any short-acting insulin
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate as the primary therapy for all patients
Continuous regular insulin infusion with careful potassium repletion
items.explanation: Diabetic ketoacidosis is corrected with a continuous regular insulin infusion and vigilant potassium replacement, because insulin drives ketone clearance and potassium falls rapidly once acidosis resolves.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Endocrine and Behavioral Medicine

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman with known Graves disease develops fever to 40 C, tachycardia at 170 beats per minute, delirium, and vomiting after surgery. TSH is suppressed and free T4 is markedly elevated. Which drug combination is the cornerstone of treatment?
options: Radioactive iodine ablation in the emergency department
Propylthiouracil as the sole agent without a beta blocker
A thionamide with a beta blocker and an iodine solution given after thionamide pretreatment
Methimazole given once daily as monotherapy
items.explanation: Thyroid storm requires a thionamide to block new hormone synthesis, iodine at least an hour later to inhibit release, and a beta blocker for the adrenergic surge, plus treatment of the trigger.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Endocrine and Behavioral Medicine

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman with autoimmune polyglandular disease presents with hypotension unresponsive to fluids, hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia, and cosyntropin stimulation produces no cortisol rise. Which therapy should be given immediately?
options: Immediate intravenous hydrocortisone with isotonic crystalloid
Hypertonic saline infusion
Fludrocortisone tablets by mouth
Subcutaneous insulin for the hypoglycemia
items.explanation: Adrenal crisis is an emergency treated at once with stress-dose intravenous hydrocortisone and fluids, and fludrocortisone is unnecessary in crisis because hydrocortisone already has mineralocorticoid activity.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Endocrine and Behavioral Medicine

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman has fatigue, constipation, polyuria, and recurrent kidney stones. Serum calcium is 12.4 mg per dL, phosphate is 2.1 mg per dL, and parathyroid hormone is elevated above the reference range. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Vitamin D toxicity from excessive supplementation
Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia
Squamous cell carcinoma producing parathyroid hormone-related peptide
Primary hyperparathyroidism from a parathyroid adenoma
items.explanation: Hypercalcemia with inappropriately elevated parathyroid hormone and low phosphate is primary hyperparathyroidism, while PTH-related peptide from malignancy would suppress intact PTH and suppress calcium excretion would suggest familial disease.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Endocrine and Behavioral Medicine

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman has a 1.8 cm solitary thyroid nodule discovered on examination. Ultrasound shows a solid isoechoic nodule without suspicious features, scintigraphy shows mildly increased uptake, and thyroid function is normal. What is the next step?
options: Immediate total thyroidectomy without tissue sampling
Radioactive iodine ablation to shrink the nodule
Repeat ultrasound in 3 years without biopsy
Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy
items.explanation: A solid nodule of 1.8 cm exceeds the threshold for tissue sampling, so ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration is indicated even with benign ultrasound features, with surgery following only if cytology is suspicious.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Endocrine and Behavioral Medicine

items.stem: A 64-year-old with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease with an eGFR of 40 has heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and an A1c of 8.6 percent on metformin alone. Which additional agent provides the greatest cardiovascular and renal benefit?
options: Glyburide, a sulfonylurea
Sitagliptin, a dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor
Dapagliflozin, a sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor
Pioglitazone, a thiazolidinedione
items.explanation: Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors reduce heart failure hospitalization and slow chronic kidney disease progression independent of glycemic control, whereas pioglitazone causes fluid retention and glyburide adds hypoglycemia risk.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Endocrine and Behavioral Medicine

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman has 8 weeks of depressed mood, anhedonia, early morning insomnia, fatigue, poor concentration, and feelings of worthlessness, with no psychotic features and no prior episodes. She wants a medication that also helps sleep and appetite and carries little sexual side effect risk. Which agent is best?
options: Nortriptyline
Mirtazapine
Fluoxetine
Bupropion
items.explanation: Mirtazapine sedates at low doses, improves appetite and weight, and carries among the lowest rates of sexual dysfunction, while bupropion can worsen insomnia and nortriptyline adds anticholinergic burden.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Endocrine and Behavioral Medicine

items.stem: A 24-year-old college student has slept 2 hours per night for 10 days yet remains energetic, talks rapidly with flight of ideas, spends recklessly, and is intensely irritable, with no depressed or psychotic episodes. Which medication is the best acute-phase choice?
options: Lithium combined with an atypical antipsychotic such as olanzapine
Alprazolam as the sole treatment
Bupropion augmentation
Escitalopram as monotherapy
items.explanation: Acute mania calls for a mood stabilizer with an antipsychotic for rapid control, while antidepressant monotherapy can destabilize mood and a benzodiazepine alone does not treat the mania.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Endocrine and Behavioral Medicine

items.stem: A 28-year-old combat veteran has recurrent distressing nightmares, avoidance of reminders, hypervigilance, and an exaggerated startle for 7 months after deployment, with intact reality testing and no substance use. Which treatment has the strongest evidence?
options: Trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy such as prolonged exposure
Olanzapine as monotherapy
Continuous daily benzodiazepine therapy
Supportive counseling without a structured technique
items.explanation: Trauma-focused cognitive behavioral approaches are first-line for posttraumatic stress disorder and produce durable symptom reduction, whereas benzodiazepines are discouraged and antipsychotics are reserved for select cases.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Endocrine and Behavioral Medicine

items.stem: A 30-year-old man with schizophrenia has persistent hallucinations and negative symptoms after two adequate trials of risperidone and olanzapine with no more than partial sedation. Which medication is most appropriate next?
options: Diphenhydramine alone for the hallucinations
Aripiprazole at a higher dose than previously tried
Fluphenazine decanoate injections with the same mechanism as the failed oral drugs
Clozapine with absolute neutrophil count monitoring
items.explanation: Clozapine is the only agent with proven benefit in treatment-resistant schizophrenia and requires absolute neutrophil count monitoring, while switching within the same receptor class rarely helps.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Endocrine and Behavioral Medicine

items.stem: A 42-year-old man who drinks 12 beers daily for years develops tremor, diaphoresis, tachycardia, and visual hallucinations 36 hours after his last drink. He is oriented but agitated, and he has had withdrawal seizures before. Which therapy is the priority?
options: Discharge home with outpatient follow-up only
Haloperidol as the only medication to prevent seizures
A benzodiazepine such as chlordiazepoxide, with thiamine given
Intravenous naloxone to reverse the withdrawal
items.explanation: Alcohol withdrawal is treated first with benzodiazepines to prevent seizures and delirium, and thiamine is given before glucose to avert Wernicke encephalopathy, while antipsychotics lower the seizure threshold.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Endocrine and Behavioral Medicine

items.stem: An 80-year-old man develops fluctuating inattention, daytime sedation with nighttime agitation, and disorganized thinking after hip surgery, resolving once an indwelling urinary catheter is removed. Which diagnosis best explains this?
options: Late-onset schizophrenia
Delirium
Major neurocognitive disorder due to Alzheimer disease
Persistent insomnia disorder
items.explanation: Acute onset with a fluctuating course, inattention, and an obvious precipitant that clears on correction is delirium, in contrast to the gradual irreversible decline of a neurocognitive disorder.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Endocrine and Behavioral Medicine

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman has had difficulty falling and staying asleep for 6 months with daytime fatigue, but she denies snoring, apnea, restless legs, or substance use and her mood is normal. Which intervention is first-line?
options: Continuous home oxygen therapy
Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia
Ambulatory polysomnography before any treatment
Nightly zolpidem on a long-term basis
items.explanation: Chronic insomnia without red flags is treated first with cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia, which has durable benefit, while sedative-hypnotics carry dependence risk and oxygen is not indicated.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Endocrine and Behavioral Medicine

items.stem: A 35-year-old man injects heroin daily and asks for treatment. He has no medical contraindications and has never used medication-assisted therapy. Which medication has the strongest evidence for reducing illicit opioid use and mortality?
options: Buprenorphine-naloxone maintenance combined with counseling
Disulfiram as monotherapy
Naltrexone without counseling or follow-up
Benzodiazepines for the duration of withdrawal
items.explanation: Buprenorphine-naloxone reduces illicit use, overdose death, and craving when paired with counseling, while benzodiazepines do not treat opioid use disorder and naltrexone requires full detoxification first.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Endocrine and Behavioral Medicine

items.stem: A 68-year-old man with small cell lung cancer has serum sodium of 118 mmol per liter, serum osmolality of 250 mOsm per kg, urine osmolality of 600 mOsm per kg, and urine sodium of 55 mmol per liter, with no edema or hypotension. Which therapy is most appropriate?
options: Fluid restriction with treatment of the underlying small cell lung cancer
Demeclocycline as the immediate first-line agent for every patient
Rapid infusion of 3 percent saline for many hours without monitoring
Oral sodium tablets with completely unrestricted water intake
items.explanation: Euvolemic hyponatremia from SIADH is corrected with free water restriction and management of the cancer, while hypertonic saline is reserved for severe neurologic symptoms because of osmotic demyelination risk.
items.reference: PANCE Content Blueprint - Endocrine and Behavioral Medicine
